fact_reason: 'the artery the European Frida clamped shut with her own fingers' (repeated as 'the clamp of her own fingers'). In The Two Fridas she holds surgical forceps (hemostat) to stop the bleeding (source: Wikipedia, The Two Fridas). Also uncertain: the sky is described as stormy left, calm right. Megan's uncorrected guess that Kahlo was in her twenties is also wrong: the painting is from 1939, when she was 31-32.
age_reason: 'Indigent charity dressed up as opportunity' is a forced required word.

fact_reason: 'Methionine, valine, proline, stop. A four-piece protein.' That is three amino acids, because the stop codon UAA adds none. Also, splitting CCAAUGGUACCGUAA from the first letter gives CCA AUG GUA CCG UAA, not the CAA UGG... frame the story attributes to 'the very first letter'.
age_reason: Age-appropriate, but the reading-frame steps are muddled ('the second grouping' vs the first).

fact_reason: 'Twenty by ten... a hundred square feet', presented as the maximum for length plus width equal to 60. 20 x 10 is 200, not 100. With L + W = 60 the maximum area is at 30 by 30 (900 sq ft), and 20 by 10 does not even total 60.
age_reason: Mature reflection, but 'sixty feet' then 'Twenty by ten... a hundred square feet' does not add up.

fact_reason: 'Sixty-one dollars and change for eight hours... which worked out to $7.25 an hour.' 8 x $7.25 = $58.00, and $61 over 8 hours is about $7.65 an hour.

'the small dark shape suspended at the painter's throat, its wings folded, its body slack'. In the painting the dead hummingbird hangs stiff with its wings outstretched like a pendant (source: Wikipedia, Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird). Also uncertain: the story describes leaves strung through the thorns.
The area between y = x + 2 and y = x^2 on [-1, 2] is given as 'Six', and the story endorses it. The integral of (x + 2 - x^2) from -1 to 2 is 9/2 = 4.5, the answer Deshawn had first.
age_reason: Story contradicts itself: Deshawn subtracts 'in the wrong order' yet gets a positive 'four and a half', and the text says the wrong order gives 'negative six', so the central lesson does not add up.

fact_reason: Sadie's tRNA card reads AUG and carries methionine, and it pairs with an mRNA stake reading UAC. Methionine's codon on the mRNA is AUG, read by a tRNA with anticodon UAC; an mRNA codon UAC codes for tyrosine, not methionine.
age_reason: Strong teleology debate, though the tRNA card/stake setup is briefly muddled.

fact_reason: The story says Owen swapped assertEquals's arguments and that swapping them back turned the test green. His call assertEquals(0, getYear()) already had expected first; the bug was a wrong expected value. Swapping argument order never changes whether assertEquals passes, it only changes the failure message.
age_reason: Plot contradicts itself: 'He had not written 0 anywhere' then reads 'Assert equals, zero comma', and swapping the arguments makes the failing test pass.

fact_reason: The story quotes the invitation as 'I shall be at your side, and I invite you, so that you may be with me' and says 'That part at least was certain.' The tablet says 'I give you a warm invitation to make sure that you come to us' and, in Claudia's hand, 'I shall expect you, sister' (source: Wikipedia, Claudia Severa, citing Tab. Vindol. 291).

'No, this counts the whole cohort... Anyone who started ninth grade with us, wherever they ended up. That's how they calculate it.' The adjusted cohort rate removes students who transfer out, emigrate or die and adds transfers in (NCES Condition of Education, ACGR indicator); the 87% figure itself is correct.
age_reason: Fits grade 12, though Priya repeats the same statistic verbatim twice, which reads a little like an info-dump.

fact_reason: 'twelve twelve-year-olds... the association had given her the Bantam house team'. Bantam is the 13-14 (U15) division; twelve-year-olds play Peewee (source: Wikipedia, Minor ice hockey).

'the first movement of Mozart's A major sonata' is analysed as sonata form with exposition, development and recapitulation. Mozart's only A major piano sonata, K. 331, opens with a theme and variations, not sonata form (source: Wikipedia, Piano Sonata No. 11 (Mozart)).
The cello's open A string is tuned to 440 Hz and its octave reads 880. The cello's A string is A3 (Wikipedia, Cello), an octave below A440, so it is 220 Hz and its octave is 440 Hz.
age_reason: Two ways of knowing suits grade 12; 'lectures seeming to adumbrate behind her eyes' is strained.

fact_reason: 'the cow was brown anyway, out here, in its hair and its skin and its milk.' A brown cow's milk is white, not brown; coat colour genes do not colour the milk.

The story presents a thrust stage as one where everything faces one way and the audience sits 'in one place', a room with a front. A thrust stage has the audience on three sides; the one-directional stage described is a proscenium.

'The carbon in the fog on the water had been corn this morning' (and later 'the faint fog... carbon that had been wheat'). The visible breath fog is condensed water vapour; the exhaled CO2 is invisible and is not in the fog.
age_reason: Fits the band, but the letter to Reese reads partly as a recap of the equation, and 'wheat' contradicts the earlier 'corn'.

fact_reason: 'divided again and got 2.9946.' 175.0 / 58.44 = 2.9945. Also, 'the swabs are reusable' is presented as fine for sterile culturing; swabs used to inoculate plates are single-use. The injected fact is stated correctly.

'Why is it a hundred and two dollars when the menu said eighty-nine?' 'Thirteen percent, added at the end.' 13% tax on $89 comes to $100.57, not $102. (The injected VAT fact and the £12 to £2 VAT calculation are correct.)

The story calls 289 g of NH3 from 51 g of H2 'impossible' and calls grams-to-moles-then-2/3 the error, then has Chase tell the class 'our answers are wrong'. 51 g H2 is about 25.5 mol, which gives 17 mol NH3, about 289 g. That answer is correct, and the product can outweigh the hydrogen because the nitrogen adds mass.
age_reason: Plot contradicts itself: the answer is 'ridiculous' at 289 g, then 'settled at 289 grams, unchanged' yet 'our answers are wrong the same way.'

fact_reason: The story says the 6.2% Social Security withholding alone explains the pay 'down to the last digit' ($73.15 to $68.62). US employers also withhold 1.45% Medicare on all wages (Wikipedia, FICA), so net pay would be about $67.55.

'quietly defaulting on two thirds of the debt' is wrong: a 65.6% yield means about a third (34.4%) was lost, not two thirds. ('eleven grams of ambition had condensed into eight' also misstates the 12.5 g theoretical yield.)
age_reason: Wry and age-appropriate; the numbers slip ('eleven grams of ambition', 'two thirds of the debt') against the 12.5 g and 65.6% given.

fact_reason: 'Camille slid the weight up the pendulum and the ticking quickened.' On a mechanical metronome, sliding the weight up slows the tempo and sliding it down speeds it up (Wikipedia, Metronome).

The gray looks 'warm where it touched the orange field, cold where it crossed the blue', and 'against the orange... it went warmer'. By Chevreul's law, which the story itself quotes correctly (Wikipedia, Chevreul), a gray next to orange shifts toward blue (cooler) and a gray next to blue shifts toward orange (warmer). The story shows the effect backwards.

'So the dam isn't the energy. The spinning is.' The narrator praises this line as the key insight, but the proton gradient (the 'dam') is the stored energy; ATP synthase's rotation turns that energy into ATP.
age_reason: Chemiosmosis explanations run long, but they are tied to his conflict with his father; 'extrinsic bribes' is slightly forced.

fact_reason: 'Elizabeth... could refuse Darcy twice.' Elizabeth refuses Darcy only once (Hunsford) and accepts his second proposal (source: Project Gutenberg text, ch. 58).

'see whether it cooled in minutes, dull and dry, without streaks... It set fast. It looked matte.' A correctly tempered test smear sets glossy; a dull or matte finish is a sign of poor temper (Wikipedia, Chocolate tempering). Sign of the same problem: the 'gray-white fan' on the break of a well-tempered bar.

The story analyses the first movement of K. 331 as a sonata-form movement with a march first theme, a development and a recapitulation. K. 331's first movement is a theme and variations, not sonata form (Wikipedia, Piano Sonata No. 11).
age_reason: Fits well; 'the score was immunology, the study of something alive done through things already dead' misuses the required word.

fact_reason: 'Others were blue, thinner, dragging down the eastern edges of continents.' Cold equatorward currents mostly run along the western edges of continents (California, Humboldt, Canary, Benguela), which is the eastern side of ocean basins (Wikipedia, Ocean current).
age_reason: Borderline-simple content (reading a map key), rescued by the value conflict between false confidence and admitting uncertainty.

fact_reason: 'Deduct the boots, claim the credit on the pass.' Canada's federal public transit tax credit was eliminated in 2017 (Wikipedia, 2017 Canadian federal budget), and an employee cannot generally deduct required work boots/clothing (CRA rule, judged on knowledge).
age_reason: Wry and age-appropriate, though Mr. Fennick's deduction-versus-credit explanation is somewhat tutorial.

fact_reason: 'He divided. Six point two percent, almost exactly.' $171 minus $152.06 is $18.94, which is about 11% of $171. Social Security at 6.2% would be $10.60.
age_reason: Good competing views on Social Security; the '$19 is six point two percent' arithmetic slip is minor.

fact_reason: 'the printed flight time shrank as the angle rose, exactly as it should if more of the speed were being spent upward.' A larger upward component makes flight time longer, not shorter. The ball also lands past the 3.8 m speed-times-time point, which cannot happen because the horizontal speed is less than the full launch speed.
age_reason: Suitable, but hard words are misused ('a small visceral gesture', 'the logos of the whole thing').

fact_reason: 'Chapter 34, the chapter with the hair and the locket and the digging.' The locket-and-hair scene is in Chapter 16, and Heathcliff describes digging to Catherine's coffin in Chapter 29. Chapter 34 covers Heathcliff's death (Gutenberg text).
age_reason: Sophisticated and suitable; 'sentience' is slightly forced.

fact_reason: 'The recapitulation announced itself when the opening theme returned in the original key' (K. 545). K. 545's recapitulation famously begins in F major, the subdominant (Wikipedia, Piano Sonata No. 16). The second theme also starts around m. 14, not m. 22, and the exposition is 28 bars, not 'sixty measures'.
age_reason: Fits grade 12, but the aside tying a physics-class essay to 'the logos of a thing' and 'small and fundable and quiet' feel forced.

fact_reason: Juliette moves her second-theme mark from m. 23 to 'four measures later, where the new material actually established itself in the dominant key', and the teacher endorses it. In K. 332, m. 23 starts a D-minor passage and the C-major second theme begins at m. 41 (Wikipedia, Piano Sonata No. 12).
age_reason: Playful and age-appropriate; 'Acquittal of a hunch takes longer' forces the required word.

fact_reason: '126 over 78 ... within the normal range under the 2017 American guideline, not hypertension.' Under the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline, normal is below 120/80; 120-129 systolic with diastolic under 80 is 'elevated' (source: Wikipedia, Hypertension, 2017 ACC/AHA table).

'the return of the first theme ... Home again, C major' and the recap transition 'stayed exactly, stubbornly, in C.' In K. 545 the recapitulation begins in F major, the subdominant (Wikipedia, Piano Sonata No. 16 (Mozart)), and the recap transition moves from F back to C.

The worked transcription is wrong: Jessica's 'AGCUUAC' is presented as her RNA for AGCTTAG, and she corrects Devon's second letter saying 'if the DNA you started with had adenine there, you write U' when that position is G. The complementary RNA of AGCTTAG is UCGAAUC; Devon's TCGAATC only needed T changed to U.
age_reason: Grade-appropriate voice and reflection, though the base-pairing walkthrough is muddled in places.

fact_reason: 'Quebec ran its own pension and parental insurance plans instead of the Canada Pension Plan and Employment Insurance.' Quebec workers still pay EI premiums, at a reduced rate (canada.ca EI premium rates 2025); only EI parental benefits are replaced by QPIP. Also adds a false claim: 'GST and QST ... had pushed a four-dollar sandwich past five' is wrong, since 5% + 9.975% (Wikipedia, Sales taxes in Canada) brings $4 to about $4.60.

'after the front door had been opened for Elijah ... Sienna stood to lead the grace after the meal' has the order backwards: the door for Elijah is opened after Barech (Wikipedia, Passover Seder). Also, 'learned all six verses' of Chad Gadya is wrong: it has about ten characters/verses, not six (Wikipedia, Chad Gadya).

The customer's gardening books are charged 13% HST ('the 6.24 appear beneath the 48.00'). Printed books in Ontario are exempt from the provincial part of HST (Wikipedia, Harmonized sales tax), so only 5% GST ($2.40) applies.
age_reason: Fits grade 12; 'the same book cost the same soul' is an odd phrasing.

fact_reason: 'the shamash lit the others, right to left, the way his grandfather had done it.' Hanukkah candles are placed right to left but lit left to right, newest candle first (Chabad.org, How to Light the Chanukah Menorah).
age_reason: Identity ambivalence fits an 18-year-old; the candle count briefly muddles with 'all eight standing in a straight line'.

fact_reason: The story says Chapter 7 of Pride and Prejudice has 'seventeen' servant appearances, two of them named (later it says 'twenty-five'). Chapter 7 mentions a servant about three times (footman and messengers), and none is named (source: Project Gutenberg text).
age_reason: Nice dual-lens reasoning; 'Seventeen appearances' later becomes 'twenty-five servants.'

fact_reason: The failing test ('expected 50, but was 40') turns green after Mathis just swaps the two arguments, and Priya confirms that the order was the bug. In JUnit, swapping expected and actual only changes the failure message; it cannot make a failing assertion pass.
age_reason: Plot loses its own logic: the key discovery is that swapping 'the fifty came first, the forty second' turns a failing test green, so the climax makes no sense to the reader.
The VAR climax contradicts itself ('No penalty... Then the referee pointed... to the spot anyway') and swaps Kessler/Keller, so it is hard to tell whose side won or lost.

fact_reason: For a thrown ball's height h(t), 'the right end beat her critical point', with the ball 'still climbing'. A thrown ball's height is a downward parabola, so an interior critical point is the global maximum and no endpoint can exceed it. The ball also cannot still be climbing after its peak.
age_reason: Well pitched, though an endpoint beating a ball's peak ('still climbing') is confusing.

fact_reason: The narrator has the gray look warm beside orange and cool beside blue, and Kaitlyn's last word is 'That's why it's two colors.' Simultaneous contrast predicts the opposite: gray beside orange shifts toward blue (cooler), and gray beside blue shifts toward orange (warmer).
age_reason: Suitable; the brief shift to Deb's point of view is odd, and 'impugn' and 'metamorphic' are forced.

fact_reason: The worked answer: 15.0 g Al with excess Br2 gives 'one hundred forty-seven grams' of AlBr3. 0.556 mol times 266.7 g/mol is about 148 g. Also, the sandwich analogy says two slices of bread make two sandwiches, when two slices make one.
age_reason: Hard words misused ('someone who habituated to cafeteria lines', 'clean method... the most trenchant thing she ever said') and the limiting-reactant epiphany does not fit problems with excess reagent.

fact_reason: 'if you took the heat away, it would come back toward red. Mostly ... it's what the principle would say.' Nobody corrects this. Le Chatelier's principle does not predict a partial return: back at the original temperature the equilibrium, and so the colour, returns to where it started. (Also, heating a sealed glass tube directly over a stove is shown as fine.)
age_reason: Uncertainty is handled well for grade 12; 'the reaction is obsolescent' misuses the required word.

fact_reason: 'the steam sublimated off the edge of the pot.' Sublimation is solid turning straight to gas; steam rising from boiling water does not sublimate.
age_reason: Tradition-versus-guidance conflict fits grade 12; 'the steam sublimated off the edge of the pot' misuses the word.

fact_reason: In K. 545 'the opening theme came back whole, in C major' at the recapitulation. The recapitulation of K. 545's first movement famously begins in F major, the subdominant (source: Wikipedia, Piano Sonata No. 16 (Mozart)); also the opening theme is not a descending scale and the development starts from the closing material in G minor.

'Her test class compiled on the first try' after calling the constructor with 250.00 while the only 'constructor' was 'public void BankAccount(double)'. With no BankAccount(double) constructor, 'new BankAccount(250.00)' does not compile; it only compiles if no argument is passed. (Also, 'void' has four letters, not 'five letters'.)

'That line is right before he's about to break up with Jordan' and 'He doesn't mention that he's from money until it matters.' In chapter 3 the 'understanding' to be broken off is with a girl back home, and Nick calls his family 'well-to-do' on the first page. He is also not 'the only one' at the funeral: Mr. Gatz, the minister, servants, the postman and Owl Eyes attend (Gutenberg text).
'The study doesn't say what it is, so I'm making it up' (question 36). Aron et al. 1997 published all 36 questions in an appendix, including the last one (source: Wikipedia, Arthur Aron).

'Pick the hummingbird... So the hummingbird's not just a symbol, it's also red hanging in green' / 'the ribbon against the branches.' The Wounded Deer has no hummingbird or ribbon; it shows a deer with Kahlo's head, arrows, trees, a broken branch and the sea (Wikipedia, The Wounded Deer).
'Seven across... Four letters, period of decline.' 'Decay,' said Olivier. 'Decay' has five letters, not four, and the story leaves it uncorrected as the last line.

After Victor 'led off with a clean single' he 'stood in' and took pitches during Reyes's at-bat, then was forced out at second. A runner on first base does not bat or take pitches, so the story misdescribes how baseball works. The Gilovich/Vallone/Tversky 1985 details are correct (Wikipedia, Hot hand).
age_reason: Strong competing-values story, though the baseball strategy passage ('take... if Victor was erased on a bunt') is muddled.

fact_reason: 'But the telegram was secret. Nobody outside the State Department read it in 1946.' This is the protagonist's claim and it goes uncorrected. In fact, Navy Secretary Forrestal sent copies of the Long Telegram across Washington, and it was widely read by military and executive leaders (Wikipedia, Long Telegram).

The story says Huck, on hearing Jim's plan to buy or steal his children, says it 'most busted the meeting' and was 'enough to make a body ashamed of the human race.' In the novel (ch. 16) Huck says 'It most froze me to hear such talk'; 'ashamed of the human race' is his reaction to the king and duke's fraud in ch. 24 (source: Project Gutenberg text).

The tax arithmetic is inconsistent: a $10.99 item totals 'eleven dollars and seventy-something' (about 7% tax), but a $10.00 item totals $11.21 (about 12% tax). One sales tax rate cannot produce both totals.
age_reason: Fits the band; 'igneous' for a worn shoe seam is forced.

fact_reason: The story states the rule as avoiding four, then endorses giving 'forty-five' (Dax approves and she gives it). Forty-five contains the number four, which the rule says to avoid.
